newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium studying report of Luxembourg laundering.
newsitem.headline: Belgium studying report of Luxembourg laundering.

text.p: Belgian tax authorities are investigating a report that foreign leaders, political parties, sects and private individuals are laundering piles of cash through bank accounts in Luxembourg.
The weekly financial newsletter Faxtuel said the accounts belonged among others to Iraqi President Saddam Hussein, Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi and Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko.

It said the investigation was prompted by a note from an assistant to Belgium's former ambassador in Luxembourg to Foreign Minister Eric Derycke, who had in turn passed it on to Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt and Justice Minister Stefaan De Clerck.

"The minister received a copy of this report from the foreign minister on January 15. After examining it he passed a copy to the relevant authorities for investigation," De Clerck's spokesman said on Monday.
He declined to give any specific details of the report, saying it was confidential.
Faxtuel also said foreign political parties -- notably German -- had secret accounts in Luxembourg, as did several cults and private Belgian citizens in order to avoid paying tax.
"It is a broad-ranging report. What concerns us is information directly involving Belgian citizens. Information about other people or organisations does not concern us," De Clerck's spokesman said.
He noted that several investigations were already under way into possible money laundering and tax evasion schemes in Luxembourg by Belgian political parties and nationals.
A foreign ministry spokesman said the report was lacking in details but had still warranted passing on.
He stressed that it was not against the law for a Belgian national to hold a foreign bank account. What was illegal was to fail to report any income from it to the tax authorities.
A spokesman for the Luxembourg bankers association laughed off the report.
"It is very difficult to make a comment on a report that is so vague," he said. "Everyone these days is mixing up money laundering, tax evasion, tax avoidance and tax planning."
Luxembourg is a well-established tax haven and international banking centre with strict -- and much cherished -- bank secrecy laws.

Several senior Belgian socialist politicians are under investigation over allegations their parties accepted bribes in the late 1980s from Italian helicopter maker Agusta and French aerospace firm Dassault, and washed the money through Luxembourg bank accounts.
Maystadt told RTBF television on Monday that the names of two Belgian politicians were among those cited in the report.
"There is one PS (Francophone Parti Socialiste) and one SP (Flemish Socialistische Partij)," he said, declining to say more.
Belgium has issued an international arrest warrant for Dassault chief Serge Dassault in an attempt to get to the bottom of the affair.

But France does not extradite its nationals, and the authorities, to the increasing anger of the Belgian government, have proved reluctant to help the Belgian investigations into the well-connected and influential industrialist.
